findings.text: The page opens by saying what Athena is, in plain words. A newcomer can say what the project is from the first paragraph.
findings.source: <header> lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why it exists: it is a worked example of Athena's output. The claim list at the end supports this well, because every claim links to exact file lines at a fixed commit.
findings.source: <header> lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: This is the landing page of Athena's site, but the title and almost all of the body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena may wonder for a moment whether they are on the right site, until they read the second lede paragraph.

The next step is easy to find: it is linked from the header and has its own section. But the install step gives no clone command and lists no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or AI model access, so a newcomer has to go to the GitHub repository to find out what they need.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: This link is meant for the project owner, yet it sits next to the newcomer's next step. A first-time reader cannot tell whether it applies to them.
findings.source: <header>: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The Start here section is clear. It defines key terms before using them ("Words used first") and walks through one task from start to finish in a numbered list. A reader who wants to understand firstmate can follow it.
findings.source: Start here / What firstmate is: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker, so that several tasks can run side by side."

findings.text: The transition cards are dense and repeat a lot of the Start here section, with terms like exit 75, guarded fast-forward and pending-close record. A newcomer will likely skim or skip them. The glossary helps, but this part reads like reference material, not an introduction.
findings.source: Transitions, card t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead. A relaunch is not deferred for capacity."

findings.text: This limits note uses Athena's internal terms ("job", "recorded boundary", "edge") without explaining them. A newcomer will not follow it, even though the point behind it, that nothing was actually run, matters.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This points to a studies/ folder but gives no link or repository context. A newcomer who has not cloned Athena gets nothing from it.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The glossary calls Done "the final state", but the States section says Reopened also ends a task. That is a small inconsistency a careful reader may notice.
findings.source: Glossary, done: "The final state: the task record is removed and the backlog close has landed." vs States: "Done and Reopened both carry the tag "ends the task""
